prospects.name: Netlogyx
prospects.subject: a real example
angles: Email 1 angle: Managed services vs project work, technical teams not built for follow-up
Email 2 angle: Who owns the follow-up role in a small MSP
Email 3 angle: What a systematic approach recovers — different industry, same problem
prospects.body:
Hi Neil,
A painting business in Adelaide recovered $177,555 from 14 jobs last year. Not new work. Quotes they'd already sent, clients who'd gone quiet. The only difference was the follow-up happened every time instead of when someone remembered.
Different industry, same dynamic. The project quotes that slip between support tickets, the migrations and refreshes that went quiet, they're revenue sitting in limbo. Made me wonder what that number looks like for an MSP your size. Worth a thought.
Atlas

prospects.name: IT Blueprint
prospects.subject: a real example
angles: Email 1 angle: CTO-as-a-Service, blueprint stage, client momentum fades
Email 2 angle: The irony of IT consultancies — optimise client systems, manual internal pipeline
Email 3 angle: When the system works, the recovery is real
prospects.body:
Hi IT Blueprint,
A painting business in Adelaide recovered $177,555 from 14 jobs last year. Quotes they'd already sent, clients who'd disappeared. Not a different sales process. Just follow-up that happened every time.
It's an odd comparison, I know. But the dynamic is the same: proposals leave your hands, the blueprint work is done, and then the waiting starts. What comes back when someone is actually watching that gap is worth knowing. Curious if that number makes you think about your own pipeline differently.
Atlas

prospects.name: Atcom Technology
prospects.subject: a real example
angles: Email 1 angle: 26 years, recurring support vs project quotes, support tickets swallow follow-up
Email 2 angle: The aging quote problem — invested time with no closure
Email 3 angle: What systematic follow-up recovers from quotes that went quiet
prospects.body:
Hi Atcom Technology,
A painting business in Adelaide recovered $177,555 from 14 jobs last year. Quotes that went quiet, clients who never replied, jobs that would have been lost. The only thing that changed was the follow-up became systematic.
In my last email I pointed out the three-week-old project quote. Same pattern. The time is already invested. The client hasn't said no. And it just sits there while the next ticket takes its place. Made me think about what a business your size might recover if every quote got the same treatment. Worth a thought.
Atlas

prospects.name: Excel Cleaning
prospects.subject: a real example
angles: Email 1 angle: Regular cleans vs one-off NDIS/end-of-lease, different timelines
Email 2 angle: How do you triage which quiet quotes are worth a second touch?
Email 3 angle: What comes back when the answer is "all of them"
prospects.body:
Hi Excel Cleaning,
A painting business in Adelaide recovered $177,555 from 14 jobs last year. Quotes they'd already sent, clients who'd gone quiet. The only change was that every quote got followed up, not just the ones that felt warm.
I raised the challenge of triaging quiet quotes: NDIS jobs waiting on funding, end-of-lease cleans where the agent is slow, quotes sitting in that middle ground between dead and live. When the follow-up is systematic, you stop having to choose. Everything gets the same treatment, and the ones that come back are often the ones you'd have let go. Curious if that changes how you think about it.
Atlas

prospects.name: Distinct Painters (Adelaide, SA)
prospects.subject: a real example
angles: Email 1 angle: Quote volume, 20 quotes/month, team of 8 painters
Email 2 angle: Owner handles all quoting AND follow-up — that split is a bottleneck
Email 3 angle: The cost of silence when the owner is both the bottleneck and the solution
prospects.body:
Hi Distinct Painters,
I reached out recently about how you handle quoting and follow-up, and the owner-operator dynamic keeps coming back to me. When the same person writing the quotes is also running the crew, quiet quotes don't just sit there. They get buried under the next three jobs.
A painting business in Adelaide recovered $177,555 from 14 jobs last year. Not new work. Quotes they'd already sent, clients who'd disappeared. The only difference was the follow-up happened every time instead of when someone had a spare minute.
Made me think about what that number might look like for a crew of your size. Curious if it resonates.
Atlas

prospects.name: Adelaide Designer Painters (Adelaide, SA)
prospects.subject: a real example
angles: Email 1 angle: Designer/specialist positioning
Email 2 angle: Specialty work means every project unique, each quote = time investment
Email 3 angle: When bespoke quotes go quiet, the sunk time is real → what's recoverable?
prospects.body:
Hi Adelaide Designer Painters,
I reached out recently about specialty work and quoting, and the time investment in designer projects keeps coming back to me. When every quote is bespoke and every project has its own scope, the hours you put into pricing are real. A quiet quote after that isn't just a maybe. It's sunk time with no return.
A painting business in Adelaide recovered $177,555 from 14 jobs last year. Same quotes they'd already sent, same clients who'd gone quiet. The only thing that changed was the follow-up became systematic instead of occasional.
Makes me wonder what that looks like for a business where every quote is a one-off. Curious if that kind of recovery number tracks at all with specialty work.
Atlas
